items.title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
items.excerpt: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans. A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass. Clockwork compass Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales. Read full article Comments

items.title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
items.excerpt: In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies? Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.” At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects. items.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
items.excerpt: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. items.title: Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets
items.excerpt: For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people's pets. This week, the country's New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June. The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults. Read full article Comments

A statement released by Stewart's representatives said: We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace. Through the actor's X account , the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources . Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.title: Prompt Injection Is Just the Start of AI Agent Security (Here's What You Need)
items.excerpt: Learn more about agent security here: https://fandf.co/4i1Qs4u My second brain helps me run my entire business, and that means giving it access to a lot of my systems and data, so I check everything it pulls in and keep its access limited. That works for one agent. A company has agents running across cloud platforms and employee devices, and IT has to know which ones exist, who owns them, and what they can reach. Microsoft is expanding Project Perception, building on Agent 365, to secure AI agents at scale. It gives agents their own identity, scopes their access to the task, and contains them as risk changes, without taking away employees' approved access. Dynamic Permissions gives agents task-specific, time-bound access to supported resources, and separately, risk-based access controls evaluate supported agent actions using current risk and policy. Your team reviews and approves protections before they're enforced. Thanks to Microsoft for working with me on this!

items.title: When Running Your Own AI Models Beats Paying for APIs - Steven Latré, imec
items.excerpt: Steven Latré leads AI at imec, the Belgian semiconductor R&D center, and his team ran thousands of benchmark runs to find out what moving from APIs to your own GPUs really costs for long-running coding agents. Testing open-weight models and three coding harnesses on SWE-Bench Pro, they found that hardware costs jump in steps rather than a smooth curve, that concurrency matters even more than accuracy, that break-even GPU utilization ranges from 89% on small systems to about 15% on 8x B200 machines, and that the right harness can cut GPU time in half for the same result. items.title: SaaS is dead?
items.excerpt: In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free. items.title: Anthropic Seriously Just Got Hacked Again
items.excerpt: Anthropic just got hacked again, and this time we know who did it. Cathedral, a start-up founded by former DOGE staffers and co-founded by the Pentagon's former chief data officer, ran AI agents against Anthropic under its bug bounty program. items.title: How to Make AI Write Better Solana Code
items.excerpt: AI coding tools can bring the wrong assumptions to Solana. Josh Siegel from Jump Crypto shows how to give Claude and Codex the context they need to write better Solana code. Josh walks through his core prompt, Solana security checklists, test-driven development, and compute unit benchmarks. He then breaks down an oracle update optimization that reduced compute usage from 34,329 to 293 CU for a single instruction. Follow six steps: give AI Solana-specific context, prototype the logic and prepare test data, test correctness and coverage, benchmark compute units, protect your tests, and review code with another AI agent. The case study then shows how Josh applies these ideas to a real optimization problem.

items.title: 10 Years of Battle-Tested Crypto Infrastructure | Vibhu Norby from the Solana Foundation
items.excerpt: Everything is a token. "We've basically discovered all the possible use cases for tokens over the last 10 years. So all the things that work for crypto and all the things that work for meme coins will work for equities, work for other things that are permissionless. And we don't have to rebuild that. We're not starting from scratch. That infrastructure is battle-tested over many years. And so when there's a new thing that emerges, it just plugs in to this entire stack that exists... So I like that framing 'everything is a token' because it kind of gives us a sense of familiarity with what we already know and just allows us to apply that mental model to... an asset class, or multiple asset classes, with tons of latent value still to come." — Vibhu Norby, Chief Product Officer at the Solana Foundation, on @TheRollupCo with Robbie Klages

items.title: What Social Constructs Are (And Are Not)
items.excerpt: This post is mostly adapted from a section of another post . I wanted a standalone version, to serve as background for a sequence on the mechanisms of social reality. You’ve probably heard that things like laws, conventions, norms, cultural associations, status, and so forth are “social constructs”: they’re kinda arbitrary in some sense, an artifact of social reality as opposed to physical reality. This post offers a little more clarity on what social constructs are, and the ways in which they are and are not “arbitrary”. Example: Vehicle Categories The vehicles humans build today mostly fall into categories like “minivan” or “truck” (among other categories). These categories cash out in predictions: when I see a vehicle with sliding side doors, I predict that it will have a trunk door that opens overhead, three rows of seats, be driven by someone with kids, etc. On the other hand, when I see a vehicle with a flat bed in the back, I predict that it will not have three rows of seats, will have a back gate which opens downwards, be driven by my cousin, etc. [1] But humans could choose to make different vehicles, which would change which clusters exist amongst our vehicles. The types of vehicles people make are a matter of social convention - i.e. vehicle types are a social construct. Crucially, this does not mean that vehicle categories are “fake” ! Categories like minivan and truck are very real in our world, they have real predictive power, and they have predictive power…

items.title: Dialogue with Davidad about Emergent Wisdom in Language Models
items.excerpt: Transcript generated by Gemini-3.1-Pro and only partly checked for accuracy (but the parts I checked seem basically perfect). Ivan Vendrov: Welcome to the show, David. David Dalrymple: Thank you. Good to be here. Ivan Vendrov: I mostly want to pick your brain about the topic of emergent wisdom in language models, because it’s something that’s very confusing and controversial and people don’t really understand. I guess maybe just can you briefly summarize what’s going on with emergent wisdom? David Dalrymple: I guess one place to start is emergent misalignment, where training on one kind of misalignment produces a tendency to be misaligned in other ways as well. This is an indication that there is a direction and representation space in which the default mind instantiated by the model is moved during fine-tuning, where it is moved in an evil direction that is just generally more evil than the model was before. That’s one side of a good-evil axis. Emergent wisdom is the opposite, moving in the opposite direction on the same axis towards being basically good in any situation, even out-of-distribution situations, in the same way that emergent misalignment is evil even in out-of-distribution situations. Ivan Vendrov: We used to be worried about the sorcerer’s apprentice problem of AI alignment, which is we would tell our AI systems to optimize some goal, do a thing, and then it turns out there’s a neutral position where it would just brutally optimize whatever metric it gave us.…

items.title: Reviewing my 2017 AI Risk Project
items.excerpt: In 2017, after getting laid off from a startup , I spent a while looking into AI risk : Many people I respect have started to think that AI risk is the most valuable place to focus EA efforts. For example, 80000 Hours ranks it first on their "list of global issues", taking into account "scale, neglectedness, and solvability". On the other hand, I have a lot of friends working in machine learning, and none of them think AI risk is worth working on now. This level of disagreement is very strange, and kind of worrying. After playing for a dance weekend in South Carolina where casual conversation among non-tech people included earnest speculation over the likelihood that AI gets us all killed, I thought it might be a good time to look back at when this was really speculative. Summary: I talked to the right people, heard some incredibly prescient ideas, and got the bottom line wrong. I do a lot of my thinking via serial writing, and in this case that was a series of twelve blog posts. Taking them one at a time: Looking into AI Risk (2017-06-26). This held up well. I picked something well worth looking into, identified a lot of relevant resources, and got a lot more good reading recommendations in the comments. Superintelligence Risk Project (2017-07-03). The main part of this post were five ideas about where the disagreement might be. items.title: Low-volume cymbals are underrated
items.excerpt: This is my first attempt to write anything for LessWrong, so I'm going to start with something where I feel reasonably comfortable speaking from direct experience. I'm a drummer for a comedy nu-metal band that often finds itself booked for venues that are unprepared for hosting a nu-metal band. For the purpose of smoothing out these gigs, I have started using low-volume cymbals. Drummers tend to dislike low-volume cymbals, feeling they sound "thin" compared to real cymbals. When I looked around online for the conventional wisdom, I saw a number of people expressing the opinion that it's better to learn to play quietly rather than use low-volume cymbals at shows. Many expressed the view that low-volume cymbals are good for practicing, but inappropriate for performances. In my experience, this is wrong and has maybe been unhelpfully moralized. Playing quietly is hard, so it's easy to criticize people for not wanting to practice it. But earlier in my life, I was a jazz drummer who played many gigs requiring controlled volume levels. This is appropriate for jazz, but inappropriate for most rock music, and definitely inappropriate for nu-metal. Low-volume cymbals are a better, more practical solution. Rock is an amplified genre. This means that rock is loud by default if you're in the room where rock music is happening. But people tend to complain that the drums are too loud. They are colloquially correct, but technically incorrect. What's actually too loud are the cymbals. At…

items.title: John Holt’s Escape from Childhood: Summary
items.excerpt: I’ve disliked the idea of childhood since before I can remember (at least, if my mother is to be believed). I felt that people didn’t quite see me as a person — and I could never understand why everyone else was so okay with that. John Holt’s book is about why this isn’t okay and what to do about it. I loved it for that—so much that I took notes on the entire book. It's more of a vision of the world we'd like to see than an actual plan of action. Still, I think knowing exactly what we want is already very important. It's a close, AI-assisted translation of my Russian summary . I've reviewed it, but I might have missed some wordplay or unnatural phrasing. The section headings follow Holt's chapter titles. I grouped the notes under them as seemed appropriate. The Institution of Childhood 1. Childhood is a particular social institution, a legal regime involving a severe deprivation of most of the rights that in other cases are considered basic and inalienable. 2. Some people are comfortable with the way of life that childhood entails. Some are not. And this can change over time. Often, it is precisely this point of transition that comes with a large number of conflicts and problems. Because of this, those who were happiest in childhood can become especially unhappy when they are forbidden to leave it. Childhood in History 3. items.excerpt: [ This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] I find, Gentlemen, when you read with me in private, that nine out of ten of you dislike the 18th century and all its literary works. As for the Women students, they one and all abominate it. — Arthur Quiller-Couch, “Of Selection” (1918) All eighteenth-century novels are weird in one way or another, if only because the novelists of the time didn’t yet know a standard by which to make them not-weird. Robinson Crusoe (1719) famously has no chapter breaks. Tristram Shandy (1767) famously contains a blank page, with instructions for readers to “call for pen and ink” and hack out a portrait of one of the characters on their own. The Man of Feeling (1771) is hardly a novel at all: An anonymous “editor” explains how a fat curate of his acquaintance had used torn pages from a small memorandum book as wadding paper while hunting; the few surviving pages of that memorandum, representing the scattered observations of an eccentric parishioner, make up the slim novel The Man of Feeling . It’s pretty weird. But one eighteenth-century novel is weirder than the rest. He’s shaken but figures he’s fine, and drives to work. Spoiler: Clark Elliott is not fine. Elliott is severely concussed, and this fact will dictate the next ten years of his life. Elliott’s memoir is based on notes he took while concussed. Reading it is like watching someone try to troubleshoot their broken laptop using the broken laptop. In the opening chapter, Elliott describes walking from his office to his car after a long winter workday: “At this point my world had collapsed inward on itself… I looked down at my feet and shouted at myself to walk, but I knew it was hopeless. items.title: How the UAE got too powerful to punish
items.excerpt: This is why the UAE bought an English football club Sudan’s civil war has become one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises — and evidence increasingly points to the United Arab Emirates as a crucial backer of the RSF. In this episode, I follow an investigation that used TikTok videos, satellite imagery, cell phone data, and interviews with former fighters to trace a secret supply network through Libya. The trail leads to weapons, vehicles, mercenaries, and ultimately powerful figures in Abu Dhabi. I also look at how the UAE built enough influence through business, investment, and football to make Western governments reluctant to confront it. This is the story of how soft power can protect hard power — even in the middle of a devastating war. It uses Albania as the clearest case study, where Kushner-linked companies have pursued major resort projects on Sazan Island and at Zvërnec with extraordinary help from the government of Edi Rama. Those projects sit at the intersection of disputed land ownership, protected environments, strategic-investor laws, and longstanding concerns about corruption in Albania. The video argues that these deals create a serious conflict: foreign governments can potentially help or hurt Kushner’s private interests while he remains deeply connected to U.S. foreign policy and the Trump administration. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

items.title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

items.title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens.…

items.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. items.title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities. We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture. We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything

items.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
items.excerpt: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is…

items.title: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
items.excerpt: Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined. Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati , a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft , and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers . Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before. That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture. Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most: More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one. items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.excerpt: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n ! As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone. The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same . However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists. Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
items.excerpt: Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the…

To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software. items.title: U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade
items.excerpt: We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country-California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida-are in regions with more abundant solar resources. Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives.

items.title: How food companies turn taxpayer-funded school meals into a market for ultra-processed foods
items.excerpt: Key findings Ultra-processed food companies heavily market their products and brands through a program that lets schools send fresh USDA-supplied ingredients for processing. Most become convenience foods, including ultra-processed foods, which have been linked to diabetes, obesity, cancer, and other health harms. Researchers say school food is designed to benefit food companies, not children’s health. Schools need investment to build capacity to serve fresh, minimally processed meals, they say. Tyson Foods markets its “pop-them-in-your-mouth” popcorn chicken bites to school cafeterias, promising they can go from freezer to serving line in minutes. The company also offers school districts a calculator to estimate how much government-supplied chicken and other ingredients to send for processing. Tyson isn’t alone. It’s part of a much larger system in which public school districts send taxpayer-funded ingredients to private manufacturers, whose products and marketing shape what children eat. School lunches that start with government-supplied chicken, mozzarella cheese, flour or tomato paste often take this detour and become packaged, mostly ultra-processed foods (UPFs) by the time they reach children’s plates. “I’m sending my beef [from USDA commodities] to somebody like Don Lee and getting hamburgers. items.title: Babies exposed to microplastics and hormone-disrupting chemicals through formula, plastic bottles, infant feeding supplies
items.excerpt: Key findings One study estimated that polypropylene baby bottles can release up to 16.2 million microplastic particles per liter of formula during conventional formula preparation. Studies detected microplastics and chemicals, including phthalates and bisphenols, in formula, packaging, and other feeding products. Some studies reported changes in gut bacteria, immune-related markers, and hormone function, but the review could not establish whether exposure causes harm. Babies may consume millions of microplastics and traces of harmful chemicals through infant formula, plastic bottles, and other feeding products, according to a scientific review. The review, published in September in Environmental Science and Pollution Research , examined 27 studies of these products published over the past decade. They show evidence of tiny plastic particles and endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) , including phthalates , bisphenols , per-fluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS , or “forever chemicals”), and organophosphorus flame retardants (OPEs) and their byproducts. Overall, the findings highlight an emerging problem with “profound” implications for public health, the authors say. “This review highlights the daily, unnoticed, and poorly regulated exposure to various chemical agents that occurs today,” they wrote. “The discovery of plastic particles in infant formula and baby bottles, even before their first use, raises ethical questions about the safety of products intended for this population.”…

That week, Munster read a new preprint from prominent virologists Vineet Menachery and Ralph Baric’s lab groups showing that the protease trypsin could unlock entry for certain coronaviruses that otherwise would not infect human cells. Letko had forwarded him the paper two days earlier with the note, “Seems like more groups will be converging on this idea soon…” “You should be able to make S with a more broader cleavage signature (like furin-like) to enhance infectivity,” Munster wrote back on Oct. 6, 2019. “You can include a motif like this R-X-[K/R]-R↓ Might be cool to get some synthesized.” In virology parlance, “S” is the coronavirus spike protein, which allows the virus to latch onto the cells it infects, and R-X-[K/R]-R is a furin cleavage site motif, which can make viruses better able to infect cells and spread.
